# Cooling the City: How Urban Design Can Tame Summer Heat

Every summer, cities become furnaces. Concrete and asphalt absorb sunlight all day and release it slowly through the night, so that urban temperatures routinely run five to ten degrees Fahrenheit hotter than surrounding countryside—a phenomenon known as the urban heat island effect. This gap is not merely uncomfortable; it is deadly. Heat kills more Americans annually than hurricanes, floods, and tornadoes combined, and its victims are disproportionately elderly residents, outdoor workers, and low-income families living in neighborhoods without air conditioning or shade. The good news is that heat is a design problem, and cities have a growing toolkit for solving it. The challenge is that every tool involves tradeoffs, and residents must decide together which burdens they are willing to bear.

## Trees: The Oldest Air Conditioner

The single most effective intervention against urban heat is also the most ancient: planting trees. A mature shade tree can lower surface temperatures beneath its canopy by twenty to forty degrees Fahrenheit, and through evapotranspiration—the process by which leaves release water vapor—it cools the surrounding air as well.
